pamphlet_excerpts: Hazards, First Aid & Safety: Dehydration, caused by lack of water in the body, can occur in cold or warm weather, anytime a person is sweating profusely and/or not drinking enough (p. 28).
Hazards, First Aid & Safety Principle 2: Avoid dehydration by drinking plenty of fluids and eating enough throughout the day to keep your body well-balanced (p. 28).
Hazards, First Aid & Safety Principle 3: If you become weary or develop a headache or body aches, or if you become confused, rest in the shade and sip water until the symptoms subside (p. 28).
Hazards, First Aid & Safety Principle 4: If the freezing continues, the area will stiffen and become grayish-white in color (p. 28).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Hazards, First Aid & Safety): To treat the victim, thaw the affected area only if there is no risk of refreezing (p. 28).
Step 2 (Hazards, First Aid & Safety): Put cold fingers under the armpit and the warm palm of your hand on frostbitten nose, ears, or cheeks (p. 28).
Step 3 (Hazards, First Aid & Safety): In a shelter, if possible, put cold feet on a companion's bare belly, or immerse the affected area in lukewarm water, no warmer than 108 degrees (p. 28).
Step 4 (Hazards, First Aid & Safety): If blisters develop, apply a large sterile dressing (p. 28).

Step 4 (Climbing Core Field Standard): Wear a properly fitted helmet when climbing above shoulder height whether you are on a rock face, tower, or artificial wall (p. 42).

Step 3 (Climbing Core Field Standard): If they don't fit together neatly, the knot is incorrectly tied (p. 53).

pamphlet_excerpts: Harness, Helmet and Gloves: Using a harness that fits properly helps make climbing and rappelling safer, more comfortable, and fun (p. 57).
Harness, Helmet and Gloves Principle 2: Commercially made climbing harnesses usually require only that you put your legs through leg loops and then secure the waists trap with a buckle (p. 57).
Harness, Helmet and Gloves Principle 3: The leg loops of some harnesses can be adjusted; you should just be able to slip two fingers between the loop and your thigh (p. 57).

Harness, Helmet and Gloves Principle 4: If the harnesses available to you are not adjustable, you will need to choose one that fits your body snugly but not tight enough to restrict circulation (p. 57).

Step 2 (Harness, Helmet and Gloves): Each tied harness must be tied exactly right every time to ensure your safety (p. 57).
Step 3 (Harness, Helmet and Gloves): There-fore, you must learn how to tie a seat harness from a qualified instructor (p. 57).
Step 4 (Harness, Helmet and Gloves): Once you have mastered tying one of these types of seat harnesses, you can use the following descriptions as reminders of the correct methods (p. 57).

pamphlet_excerpts: Climbing Directly Belay Rope: Climbing: Verbal Signals for Climbers and Be layers Verbal signals allow a climber and a be layer to communicate and work together as a team even if they cannot (p. 65).
Climbing Directly Belay Rope Principle 2: Climbing Principle 2: Get in the habit of using verbal signals every time you are climbing or belaying (p. 65).

Climbing Directly Belay Rope Principle 3: Climbing Principle 3: Arrange the rope so that your stronger hand (usually your right hand if you are right-handed) will be the brake hand, the hand closest to the free end (p. 65).
Climbing Directly Belay Rope Principle 4: Climbing Principle 4: Exchange verbal signals (see the boxed text later in this chapter) with a climber (p. 65).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 (Climbing Directly Belay Rope): Step 1 (Climbing): As the climber ascends, pull through the belay device any slack that forms in the rope, and let the loose rope pile up next to your feet (p. 65).
Step 2 (Climbing Directly Belay Rope): Step 2 (Climbing): While holding the rope firmly with your brake hand, slide your guide hand out along the rope (p. 65).
Step 3 (Climbing Directly Belay Rope): Step 3 (Climbing): Keeping slack in the rope to a minimum will limit the length of a fall if the climber slips (p. 65).
Step 4 (Climbing Directly Belay Rope): Step 4 (Climbing): Running the rope through a belay device allows a be layer to stop a fall easily, just by moving the belay rope to one side (p. 65).
